chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Ibn Mahboub, from Dawood al-Raqqi, who said:
I heard Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) saying: 'Fear Allah and let not some of you envy others.'

Indeed, from the laws of Isa ibn Maryam was traveling about in the lands, so he went out in one of his tours and with him was a man from his companions of short stature, and he used to frequently accompany Isa (peace be upon him).
So when Isa reached the sea, he said: 'In the Name of Allah,' with correct certainty from him, and he walked upon the back of the water.

So the short man said when he looked at Isa (peace be upon him) risking it, 'In the Name of Allah' with correct certainty from him. So he walked upon the water and caught up with Isa (peace be upon him).
Then self-conceitedness entered into himself, so he said (to himself), 'This is Isa, the Spirit of Allah, walking upon the water and I am walking upon the water. So what is his merit over me?'
So he sank into the water, and he cried for help to Isa. So he grabbed him from the water and extracted him.

Then he said to him: 'What did you say, O Shortie!?' He said, 'I said, 'This is the Spirit of Allah, walking upon the water, and I am walking upon the water', and the self-conceitedness entered me due to that'.

So Isa said to him: 'You had placed yourself in other than the place which Allah had Placed you in, therefore Allah Detested you upon what you said. So repent to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, from what you said'.
So the man repented and returned to his status which Allah had Placed him in. Therefore, fear Allah and you should not envy each other.

key_terms.السَّيْحُ: Traveling or touring in the land
key_terms.الْعُجْبُ: Self-conceit or pride in one's own status
key_terms.رُوحُ اللَّهِ: The Spirit of Allah (a title for Isa)

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual consequence of envy and self-conceit according to the story of Isa and his companion?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) uses the story of Isa (AS) to illustrate how *ujb* (self-conceit) arises from comparing one's own limited status to a prophet's divine station, leading to spiritual sinking. The short companion’s mimicry highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on recognizing one's ordained place (*martaba*) in the cosmic order, where pride disrupts the balance of humility. This serves as a practical warning against envy (*hasad*) not just as jealousy of others, but as the internal arrogance of elevating oneself beyond one's created nature.
